title: Surface modification of CuO nanoflake with Co3O4 nanowire for oxygen evolution reaction and electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in water to syngas
abstract: Transition metal oxides with hierarchical structures that grow on conductive substrates directly, which have been considered as promising catalysts for electrochemical catalysis. In this study, we used a stepwise synthesis method to prepare CuO nanoflake @Co3O4 nanowire composite nano-arrays (denote as CuO/Co3O4 composite), which show an excellent electrochemical performance. In the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), the CuO/Co3O4 composite shows lower overpotential of 450mV at the current density of 50mA cm 2 and a smaller Tafel slope of 42mV dec 1 in KOH solution (1M, pH1⁄4 13.7). In the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction, the prepared CuO/Co3O4 composite showed better CO selectivity in KHCO3 aqueous solution (0.1M, CO2 saturated), the corresponding Faradaic efficiency of CO product reached 35.4%, and the product ratio of H2 to CO was controlled by changing the potential values. The synthesis strategy reported here opens a way for designing high-performance electrodes for electrochemical catalysis and also provides new ideas for the construction of overall reaction (CO2 þ H2O / CO þ O2). © 2019 Elsevier Ltd. a b s t r a c t
Transition metal oxides with hierarchical structures that grow on conductive substrates directly, which have been considered as promising catalysts for electrochemical catalysis. In this study, we used a stepwise synthesis method to prepare CuO nanoflake @Co3O4 nanowire composite nano-arrays (denote as CuO/Co3O4 composite), which show an excellent electrochemical performance. In the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), the CuO/Co3O4 composite shows lower overpotential of 450mV at the current density of 50mA cm 2 and a smaller Tafel slope of 42mV dec 1 in KOH solution (1M, pH¼ 13.7). In the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction, the prepared CuO/Co3O4 composite showed better CO selectivity in KHCO3 aqueous solution (0.1M, CO2 saturated), the corresponding Faradaic efficiency of CO product reached 35.4%, and the product ratio of H2 to CO was controlled by changing the potential values. The synthesis strategy reported here opens a way for designing high-performance electrodes for electrochemical catalysis and also provides new ideas for the construction of overall reaction (CO2 þ H2O / CO þ O2).

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
With the rapid development of modern industry and severe environmental contamination problems, people's demand for clean and renewable energy is increasing [1e3]. Due to the high calorific value of hydrogen and environmental protection, hydrogen can fully meet these two requirements [4]. The electrochemical splitting water in the electrolytic cell is considered to be a cleaner route for the large-scale production of hydrogen [5e8]. Electrocatalytic water splitting reaction includes two half reactions, denote as oxygen evolution reaction (OER: 2H2O / 4Hþ þ O2 þ 4e ) and the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER: 2Hþ þ 2e / H2) [9,10]. Due to the OER reaction contains a complex 4e /4Hþ transfer process, the hydrogen produced by water splitting is mainly limited by the anodic oxygen evolution kinetics [11,12]. Therefore, efficient water oxidation catalysts are essential for accelerating the reaction kinetics and reducing the overpotential [13]. To date, precious metal oxides (such as RuO2 and IrO2) have been considered to be themost
heng).
effective electrocatalysts for OER [14,15]. As one of the main products of combustion, carbon dioxide
(CO2) is considered as a direct cause of global warming, leading to a greenhouse effect and rising sea levels [16]. The prospects of economical and sustainable recycling of CO2 have attracted widespread attention around the world [17,18]. The electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2RR) to fuels and chemicals is one of the commonly usedmethods, which the reduction products are usually carbonmonoxide (CO) [19,20], methane (CH4) [21], ethylene (C2H4) [22], formic acid (HCOOH) [23], ethanol (CH3CH2OH) [24] and other carbon-containing compounds [25]. Syngas (H2 and CO gas) is a key industrial raw material for the production of bulk chemicals (such as methanol, ethanol, ethylene glycol, etc.) and synthetic fuels [26,27]. Syngas is basically derived from non-renewable resources such as methane (CH4) and coal [28]. Provided that CO2 is used as a renewable energy source, it would be particularly attractive to use electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in water to produce a syngas [29,30]. After that, the syngas as a feed stock is used to synthesize liquid fuels or other hydrocarbons under suitable conditions through a Fischer-Tropsch (F-T) synthesis reaction [31]. In general, noble metals (Au, Ag, Pd) are used to selectively convert CO2 to above products, and it is necessary to operate at a considerable
overpotential, and even some require electrolyte additives such as ionic liquids [32e34].
Therefore, developing a catalyst which is inexpensive, high selectivity, and good stability at a low overpotential is the top priority. Due to the reversible surface redox reaction, the first row transition metal oxides/hydroxides (such as Co3O4, NiFe LDH) which has the advantages of low cost, earth abundance and excellent catalytic performance, showing potential applications such as energy conversion and storage, which may expected to replace precious metals [35e39]. For OER, Liu's group has synthesized ε-MnO2 microspheres with superior OER activity, which exhibit the low overpotential of 420mV (at j¼ 10mA cm 2) [40]. Du et al. [41] have synthesized CuO nanosheets for OER with a low overpotential of 420mV at 10mA cm 2. For CO2RR, Tang et al. [42] have synthesized a highly active Co3O4 hexagonal platelets with the CO Faradaic efficiency of 77.1%. Zhang and coworkers reported three dimensional (3D) hierarchical mesoporous SnO2 nanosheets on carbon cloth for CO2RR, which exhibit a partial current density of 45mA cm 2 at an overpotential of 0.88 V with high Faradaic efficiency of formate of 87% [43]. However, the activity based on a single transition metal oxide electrocatalyst still needs to improve. If one can synthesize a catalyst with a specific core-shell 3D heterostructure, it can not only increase the surface area and active sites, but it can also promote the diffusion of the reactants and generated gases simultaneously [44]. Last but not least, these heterogeneous catalysts can exhibit synergy by reinforcing or modifying the core and shell materials [13]. For instance, Sun's group reported Cu nanorod @(Cu(OH)2eCuO) nanosheet sample with an overpotential of 417mV at a current density of 10mA cm 2 for OER [45]. Schreier et al. [46] have synthesized SnO2-modified CuO nanowires as electrode for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction with the Faradaic efficiency of CO of 84% which is much higher than that of pure CuO. Our group recently reported a self-supported hierarchical CuOx@Co3O4 heterostructures material (in-situ grown on Cu foam) with excellent catalytic performance, and at a current density of 50mA cm 2 it shows extremely low overpotentials of 240mV and 242mV for OER and HER, respectively [47].
In this work, we synthesize hierarchical CuO nanoflake arrays on Cu foil through a facile hydrothermal method and then Co(OH)2 nanonwire arrays were controllably loaded on the CuO nanoflake arrays. Awell-ordered CuO nanoflake@Co3O4 nanonwire composite nano-arrays based electrode were obtained after thermal treatment as a bi-functional catalyst used for OER and CO2RR. The water splitting reaction was performed in 1M KOH solution with an overpotential of 450mV at a current density of 50mA cm 2. The stability tests for OER showed that the composite electrode was stable under alkaline conditions for more than 10 h. The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 was performed at a voltage range of 1.2 V to 1.8 V (vs. SCE) in 0.1M KHCO3, and the Faradaic efficiency of CO was 35.4% at a voltage of 1.6 V vs. SCE.

sections.heading: 2.1.1. Material and chemicals
sections.text:
All the chemicals involving cobalt nitrate hexahydrate (Co(N-
O3)2$6H2O, 99%), urea (CO(NH2)2, 99%), ammonium fluoride (NH4F, 98%), ammonium persulfate ((NH4)2S2O8, 98%), potassium hydroxide (KOH, 99%), sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3, 99.8%) were used without further purification purchasing from Aladdin Co., Ltd. The Cu foil (0.1mm thickness) was obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Cu foil was washed with 6M HCl, absolute ethanol and water thoroughly prior to use. All electrolyte solutions were prepared with deionized water (DI).

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis of CuO nanoflake arrays
sections.text: The hierarchical CuO nanoflake on Cu foil was prepared by a facile hydrothermal method. First, 0.5 g (NH4)2S2O8 and 2.0 g NaOH were successively dissolved to 20mL DI and then the mixture was sonicated for 30min, the mixture was transferred into a Teflonlined stainless steel autoclave (25mL). Then, the preprocessed Cu foils (1.0 2.5 cm2) were carefully immersed into the autoclave and the autoclave was capped tightly and maintained at 80 C for 10 h. Finally, the resulted black CuO nanoflake was taken out and then washed with water and ethanol, followed by dried in air for further characterization.

sections.heading: 2.3. Synthesis of Co3O4 nanowire arrays
sections.text: Typically, Co(NO3)2$6H2O (2mmol), CO(NH2)2 (5mmol) and NH4F (4mmol) were mixed in 20mL aqueous solution at room temperature and stirred until all the reagents were dissolved (denote A aqueous solution). Then, the solution was transferred to an autoclave (25mL). A piece of Cu foil (1 2.5 cm2) was immersed into the reaction solution and the autoclave was sealed tightly and maintained at 100 C for 12 h. After cooling to room temperature naturally, the precursor was rinsed with DI for at least 3 times and then dried in the air. Co3O4 nanowire arrays were synthesized by annealing of the precursor in air at 350 C for 4 hwith a heating rate of 1 C min 1, and naturally cooled to room temperature.

sections.heading: 2.4. Synthesis of CuO/Co3O4 composites
sections.text: The above-prepared CuO nanoflake was immersed in A aqueous solution, and the reaction conditions were consistent with those described above. Then the CuO/Co3O4 composites were obtained.

sections.heading: 2.5. Characterizations
sections.text: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images were collected on the JEM-2100 transmission electron microscope from JEOL at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. Morphology images and elemental composition were recorded on a scanning electron microscope (SEM, S4800) under an accelerating voltage of 15 kV which equipped with an energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analyzer. The elemental content of the material can be measured on an energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) from Oxford instruments Co. Ltd.. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded on a X-ray diffractometer (Bruker AXS D8 Advance) with 2q ranging between 20 and 80 using Cu Ka radiation (l¼ 1.54 Å). The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were carried out on the Thermo Scientific Escalab 250 Xi electron spectrometer with an Al Ka X-ray source. And the binding energies were adjusted according to C1s¼ 284.6 eV. Raman spectra were obtained on the Renishaw confocal laser micro-Raman spectrometer (United Kingdom, UK) with the He-Ne laser excitation wavelength of 532 nm.

sections.heading: 2.6. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
Electrochemical activity tests for OER and CO2RR were performed on CHI660E (Chenhua, Shanghai, China) workstation in a typical three-electrode system. The as-prepared samples grown on Cu foil could be used as the working electrodes directly. The obtained samples showed loaded mass of 1.4mg cm 2, 2.6mg cm 2 and 4mg cm 2 for CuO, Co3O4 and CuO/Co3O4, respectively. In the OER tests, the Pt foil was served as the counter electrode, the Ag/ AgCl electrode was employed as a reference electrode and the electrolyte was a 1M KOH (pH¼ 13.7) aqueous solution. Linear
sweep voltagrammetry (LSV) was performed at a scan rate of 5mV s 1 after bubbling with N2 at least for 30min, and all the LSV plots were corrected with 80% iR-compensation. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed at 1.80 V vs. RHE in the frequency ranges from 105 Hz to 10 2 Hz with an AC voltage of 5mV. The Hg/HgO electrode was used as a reference electrode for the stability test of OER. The chronopotentiometry (CP) curve was recorded under a fixed current density of 50mA cm 2. The controlled potential electrolysis (CPE) was carried out in a hermetic electrochemical cell at a fixed potential of 1.8 V vs. RHE, which used to evaluate the stability of the electrode and Faradaic efficiency. Before stability test, the electrolytewas bubbledwith N2 for 30min. During CPE, the amount of O2 evolved was quantified by gas chromatography (GC), where the carrier gas was N2, column was a molecular sieve column and detector was a TCD. The test results were shown against the RHE (reversible hydrogen electrode): ERHE¼ EAg/AgCl þ 0.197 þ 0.0591 pH. Electrochemical surface area (ECSA) was calculated by measuring the electrochemical doublelayer capacitance (Cdl) depending on the scan rate dependence of the CVs. The non-Faradaic potential rangewas 1.01e1.31 V (vs. RHE) for the cyclic voltammetry (CV) at different scan rates (50, 60, 70, 80 and 90mV s 1) which can determine the Cdl. In the CO2RR tests, The electrolytic cell contained 75mL of space, including 20mL of 0.1M NaHCO3 electrolyte and about 55mL headspace. The reference electrode and counter electrode were Hg/Hg2Cl2 (3M KCl solution) and carbon rod, respectively, and the synthesized nano-array samples grown on Cu foil were used as the working electrodes. Before electrolysis, the electrolyte was bubbled with CO2 for 40min at a rate of 10 sccm. Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to syngas was performed on different constant potentials for 1800 s. The concentration of CO and H2 productions were analyzed by gas chromatograph (GC-2060), respectively. The gas products were analyzed by a TCD (thermal conductivity detector) for H2 and a FID (flame ionization detector) for CO and hydrocarbons. Assuming that two electrons are required to produce a molecule of CO or a molecule of H2, the Faraday efficiency (FE) is calculated as follows: FE¼ 2 F n (CO)/Q¼ 2 F n (CO)/(I t), FE¼ 2 F n(H2)/ Q¼ 2 F n(H2)/(I t), where F¼ 96500 C/mol. The composition of the liquid samples were examined using a Bruker AVANCE III 400MHz nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer (1H NMR).

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
As shown in Scheme 1, the CuO/Co3O4 composite was synthesized via facile methods, which was grown on Cu foil directly. The resulting material was confirmed by XRD measurement to verify the crystal phase and structure. The crystal phase and structure of the resulted material were characterized by XRD measurement. Fig. 1 shows that XRD pattern of CuO/Co3O4 composite. The two major diffraction peaks at ~35.5 and ~38.6 belong to the (11-1) and (111) crystal planes of monoclinic phase of CuO (JCPDS No. 48- 1548), respectively [48]. And another five predominant diffraction peaks located at 31.3 , 36.8 , 44.8 , 59.4 and 65.2 corresponding to the (220), (311), (400), (511) and (440) crystal planes of cubic spinel phase of Co3O4 (JCPDS No. 42-1467), respectively [49]. EDX spectrum (Fig. S1) also demonstrates the existence of Co, Cu and O elements in CuO/Co3O4 composite, indicating its high purity. The XRD pattern of Co3O4 nanowire arrays (Co3O4-NWA) agrees well with that typical Co3O4 (Fig. S2) [50]. The as-synthesized CuO nanoflake arrays (CuO-NFA) were not scraped off the Cu foil, which was directly subjected to XRD measurement using the Cu foil as a substrate. Fig. S3 shows that three strong peaks at 43.3 , 50.4 and 74.1 are assigned to the (111), (200) and (220) planes of the Cu foil substrate (JCPDS: 04-0836), respectively [51]. And the rest of the diffraction peaks correspond to the CuO monoclinic phase exactly.
Then the morphologies of the samples were characterized by SEM and TEMmeasurements. Fig. 1 b and c display the morphology of CuO/Co3O4 composite. It can be clearly seen that Co3O4 nanowires uniformly enclose CuO nanoflakes. Besides, the space among the Co3O4 nanowires should be conducive to the diffusion of reactants and generated gases. At the same time, the morphology of the composite array should facilitate the exposure of more catalytically active sites. As shown in Fig. 1 d-f, the Co element completely covers the visible region, while the Cu element only appears in a specific region, indicating that the Co-based material well wraps around the Cu-based material. The nanowire structure of Co3O4 can be clearly seen in Fig. S4a and Fig. 4b, and CuO is a nanoflake structure in Fig. S5a and Fig. 5b. To further study the morphologies of the materials, the CuO/Co3O4 composite and the corresponding pure CuO and Co3O4 materials were characterized by TEM. Since the Co3O4 nanowires are completely covered on the CuO nanoflakes, it can be seen from Fig. 1g that the diameter of the Co3O4 nanowire on the surface of the composite is approximately 50 nm. And Fig. 1h reveals that lattice fringes of two different materials, in which the well-resolved two clear adjoining lattice fringes of 0.28 nm and 0.24 nm corresponding to the (110) plane of CuO and the (311) plane of Co3O4 [48,52]. The corresponding selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) image of CuO/Co3O4 composite is shown in Fig. 1i, which is in good agreement with the XRD pattern. The TEM and HRTEM images of Co3O4-NWA (Fig. S4c and d) and CuO-NFA (Fig. S5c and d) correspond to pure Co3O4 and pure CuO, respectively.
In order to verify the valence states of CuO/Co3O4 composite, XPS measurements were further performed. As shown in Fig. 2a, a full XPS spectrum can confirm the presence of Co, Cu and O elements. Fig. 2b shows that, the Co 2p of the CuO/Co3O4 composite has a couple of peaks located at 795.1 eV and 780.0 eV, which is corresponding to Co 2p1/2 and Co 2p3/2, respectively [53]. And the Co 2p of the composite was de-convoluted into spin-orbit doublets successfully and the fitting peaks at 798.2 eV and 782.3 eV are assigned to Co2þ, while the other peaks with the binding energies of 795.3 eV and 779.7 eV belong to Co3þ [54]. Fig. 2c depicts that the high resolution XPS spectrum of Cu 2p of the composite. Twomajor peaks at ~953.9 and ~933.8 eV are assigned to Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2, respectively, which is in complete accord with the typical characteristics of Cu(II) in CuO [55]. As for O element, the O 1s fitting peaks at 529.8 eV and 531.7 eV are observed (Fig. 2d), which belong to the O atoms of CuO and Co3O4 together due to the coincidence of their peak positions [52,56]. The molecular structure of the CuO/ Co3O4 composite was further studied by Raman spectroscopy. As can be seen from Fig. S6, Co3O4 material has four Raman peaks around at 190, 466, 505 and 667 cm 1, where the Raman shifts at 190 cm 1 and 667 cm 1 belong to Raman vibrations of Co2þ-O2 and Co3þ-O2 respectively [57,58]. The CuO material has two Raman bands, a strong band appeared at ~278 cm 1 and a weak band around 325 cm 1, which can be assigned to the Ag mode and Bg mode, respectively [59].
The OER catalytic performance was assessed by using a CuO/ Co3O4 composite as a working electrode in a three-electrode system, and compared with the properties of Co3O4-NWA and CuONFA at 1M KOH. Fig. 3a shows that the LSV plots of the asobtained electrodes with 80% iR-compensation. The CuO/Co3O4 composite shows an excellent catalytic activity with a low overpotential of 450mV at 50mA cm 2, which is 20 and 110mV lower than that of Co3O4-NWA and CuO-NFA, and even lower than that of Co3O4 and CuO materials reported recently. For example, Co3O4/ SWNTS (h¼ 595mV at 10mA cm 2 in 1.0M KOH solution) [60], Co3O4 powder samples (h¼ 490mV at 10mA cm 2 in 1.0M KOH) [61], Co3O4 hollow polyhedrons (h¼ 500mV at 10mA cm 2 in 1.0M KOH solution) [62] and CuO NSDs/CF (h¼ 390mV at
10mA cm 2 in 1.0M NaOH solution) [63], annealed CuO (h¼ 430mV for 1.0mA cm 2 in 1.0M KOH) [48], CuOx-NLs (h¼ 450mV at 10mA cm 2 in 0.2M carbonate buffer) [64]. The CuO/Co3O4 composite exhibits a high current density of 113mA cm 2 at the fixed potential of 1.70 V vs. RHE, which is much higher than Co3O4-NWA (50mA cm 2 at 1.70 V vs. RHE) and CuONFA (6mA cm 2 at 1.70 V vs. RHE). Furthermore, the Tafel plots corresponding to the LSV plots are shown in Fig. 3b. Fitted Tafel curves according to Tafel equation: h¼ b log j þ a, where h is the overpotential, j represents the current density and b denotes the Tafel slope [65]. The CuO/Co3O4 composite exhibits a Tafel slope of 42mV dec 1, while the Co3O4-NWA and CuO-NFA show the Tafel
slopes of 147mV dec 1 and 80mV dec 1, respectively, indicating that the CuO/Co3O4 composite is a more favorable catalyst for OER.
Interface charge transfer was studied by electrochemical impedance spectrum (EIS) measurement. In order to understand the ability of the interfacial charge transfer in the OER process, the charge transfer resistance (Rct) of each electrode can be obtained from a Nyquist diagram (Fig. 3c). It can be seen that CuO/Co3O4 composite shows smaller Rct (0.33U) than that of Co3O4-NWA (0.55U) and CuO-NFA (1.31U), implying that CuO/Co3O4 composite has faster charge transfer rate in OER. The effective active surface area (ECSA) can be evaluated by an electrochemical double-layer capacitor (Cdl) and a surface roughness factor (Rf). Therefore, we
calculated Cdl via performing CV experiments, which is linearly proportional to ECSA. The CV plots were performed at a potential range of 1.01e1.31 V vs. RHE in non-Faradaic region (Fig. S7a-c). Accordingly, as shown in Fig. 3d, the Cdl for CuO/Co3O4 composite is calculated as 45.6mF cm 2, which is higher than that of Co3O4NWA (34mF cm 2) and CuO-NFA (6.9mF cm 2). The corresponding ECSA of CuO/Co3O4 composite is 1140 cm2, which has a larger surface area and more exposed active sites. The stability tests were performed by CP and CPE, which are the quantitative standard for evaluating the practical application of the electrocatalysts. In Fig. 4a, the CuO/Co3O4 composite shows good stability at a current density of 50mA cm 2 for 10 h. As shown in Fig. 4b, CPE was applied at 1.8 V vs. RHEwithout iR correction, after 10 h, the current density decreased by approximately 15.2%. During electrolysis, the generated oxygen has a Faradaic efficiency of 95% (Fig. S8). Fig. S9 shows that the LSV curve after 10 h electrolysis was not much different from the LSV curve before 10 h electrolysis, with a slight loss of the current density. In addition, peaks at 932.5 eV and 934.1 eV are assigned to Cu2þ and Cu3þ species, respectively in Fig. S10. Clearly, the Cu2p3/2 peak shifted to the peaks at 933.5 eV and 935.1 eV respectively after 10 h of electrolysis at 1.8 V vs. RHE, implying that the Cu2þ in the CuO/Co3O4 composite was converted to the Cu3þ species [13,66]. According to a reported article, the Cu3þ
species is a novel catalytically active material for OER [67]. As described above, CuO/Co3O4 composite has a unique 3D internet structure and good electrochemical activity. The electrocatalytic activity of CuO/Co3O4 composite for the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) was studied in CO2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 using a three-electrode cell. Cu foil was chosen as the support substrate due to its good electrical conductivity. The LSV plots of CuO/Co3O4 composite, along with pure Co3O4, CuO and Cu foil electrodes are
shown in Fig. 5a. It can be obviously seen that the Cu foil as a substrate has no significant influence on the CO2RR. At a potential of 1.8 V vs. SCE, the corresponding current density is only 5.5mA cm 2, which is much lower than that of other electrodes. Two significant CO2RR catalytic current densities for CuO/ Co3O4 (blue line) and CuO (black line) materials can be observed at 0.9 V vs. SCE in Fig. 5a. However, for pure Co3O4, there is no obvious CO2RR current density in Fig. 5a (red line) at 1.1 V vs. SCE. At 1.1 V to 1.3 V vs. SCE, the catalytic current curves of CuO/ Co3O4 and CuO materials are almost matching together, and after 1.4 V vs. SCE, it can be seen that the catalytic current of CuO/ Co3O4 composite is greater than that of CuO material. All in all, it can be seen from the LSV curves that CuO/Co3O4 composite shows a better catalytic performance between 0.9 V and 1.8 V vs. SCE, which is higher than that of pure Co3O4 and CuO materials. Fig. 5b shows that the CO partial current density of CuO/Co3O4 composite, which can be seen the current density increased linearly between 1.2 V and 1.8 V.
The determination of the reduction products was performed by controlled potential electrolysis (CPE) measurements after 1800 s (Fig. 5c). CO and H2 were the only two detected gas products which quantified by on-line gas chromatography (Fig. S11). And there were no liquid products in the electrolyte after the CO2RR measurement which were detected by 1H NMR spectroscopy (Fig. S12). As shown in Fig. 5d, the CuO/Co3O4 composite achieved the highest Faradaic efficiency of CO of 35.4% at 1.6 V vs. SCE, and the corresponding H2 Faradaic efficiency was 61.8%. However, the Faradaic efficiency of CO was only 22.8% at 1.2 V vs. SCE. Co3O4 nanowire arrays reached the highest CO Faradaic efficiency of 30.2% at 1.4 V vs. SCE, and the Faradaic efficiency of H2 was up to 66.4% (Fig. S13). And the Faradaic efficiency of CO and H2 of the CuO nanoflake
arrays were 31.5% and 64.1% at 1.4 V vs. SCE, respectively (Fig. S15). It can be seen that the highest Faradaic efficiency of CO for the CuO/Co3O4 composite electrode is 5.2% and 3.9% higher than that of the Co3O4 electrode and the CuO electrode, respectively. The above results indicate that the selectivity of the catalyst plays a crucial role in the 0.1M KHCO3 aqueous solution under the saturation of CO2. Therefore, a series of different ratios between H2 and CO can be prepared according to industrial use by controlling the voltage of the electrolysis process. The long-term stability of CuO/ Co3O4 composite was measured by potentiostatic electrolysis for 10 h at 1.6 V vs. SCE (Fig. 6). The results showed that there was no
significant decrease of the catalytic current density after 10 h, indicating excellent long-term stability of the CuO/Co3O4 composite.
The CuO/Co3O4 composite as bi-functional catalyst has some good electrochemical performance, which may be attributed to some factors. Firstly, the free-standing Cu foil has excellent electrical conductivity and facilitates electron transport. Then, direct growth of the array on the Cu foil has a strong adhesion, ensuring close contact between the Cu foil and the array, and efficient electron transport. Thirdly, the composite array has a unique open 3D structure, which exposes more active sites, increases the contact
area between the electrode and the electrolyte, and significantly shortens the diffusion paths of ions and electrons, thereby ensuring electrochemical utilization. Finally, it may be due to the generation of Cu3þ species that make the electrocatalytic effect better.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In conclusion, we have prepared a composite nano-arrays using in-situ growth method, thereby significantly improving its electrochemical performance. Combining the advantages of a 3D
composite array structure and a conductive substrate, the CuO/ Co3O4 composite is an ideal choice for electrochemical devices. When used as an OER catalyst, the synergistic effect between the CuO/Co3O4 composite and the layered structure of the composite array electrode proved its excellent performance. CuO/Co3O4 composite as a highly efficient catalyst for water splitting also has excellent electrocatalytic activity, low overpotential, low Tafel slope, large electrochemical active surface area, and good stability. At the same time, the stability of CuO/Co3O4 composite at 1.6 V vs. SCE did not change significantly over 10 h. We believe that the potential application of this composite catalyst design and synthesis in various electrochemical energy conversion devices is very promising. As a bi-functional catalyst, it also lays a foundation for the construction of the overall reaction (CO2 þ 2H2O / CO þ 2H2 þ 3/2O2).
